title: Gas Prices Have Jumped 42 Per Cent in One Year. American Drivers Will Pay $700 More. Immigrant Families Are Absorbing the Worst of It.
excerpt: The national average has hit $4.33 a gallon, with California above $6. For NRI households already stretched between remittances, tuition, and groceries, this summer at the pump will be the most expensive in recent memory.
body:
The national average price of regular unleaded gasoline in the United States is now $4.33 a gallon. A year ago, it was $3.05. That is a 42 per cent increase in twelve months, and it is being driven almost entirely by the war between the United States and Iran that began on February 28 and has kept the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil supply passes — effectively closed.

For most American families, this is an irritation. For immigrant families — particularly South Asian households juggling remittances, children's tuition, mortgage payments, and the fixed costs of maintaining life across two countries — it is becoming a genuine financial strain.

## The Numbers

A study released this week by iSeeCars, an automotive research firm, calculated that drivers of gas-powered vehicles will pay an average of $706 more for fuel over the course of 2026 compared to pre-war prices. That figure is based on the January-to-April price trajectory, during which the national average surged 46 per cent from $2.81 to $4.10 a gallon. Since then, prices have climbed further.

In California, where a significant share of the Indian diaspora is concentrated, the average price has reached $6.03 a gallon — nearly double the national figure from a year ago. In states like Texas, where prices remain comparatively lower at $3.82, the pain is less acute but still meaningful for families driving long suburban commutes.

The real fear is that prices have further to climb. Gasoline inventories have fallen for 15 consecutive weeks, the longest such streak in recent memory, drawing national stockpiles to their lowest seasonal level since 2014. If the Strait of Hormuz remains closed into late summer, and seasonal driving demand peaks as it typically does in July and August, analysts warn that the national average could approach or exceed the all-time record of $5.03 set in June 2022 during the Russia-Ukraine crisis.

## Where It Hits Hardest

The arithmetic of higher gas prices falls unevenly. For a two-income household in suburban Houston or northern New Jersey where both adults commute 30 miles each way, an extra $700 a year in fuel costs is manageable but unwelcome. For a single-income family supporting elderly parents in India through monthly remittances, it is the expense that pushes the budget from tight to untenable.

The cost of gasoline does not stay at the pump. Diesel prices, which have risen to $5.84 a gallon in some states, directly affect the cost of shipping food, goods, and materials. Grocery prices, which typically lag fuel prices by three to six months, are expected to rise further through the autumn. For families that already spend a disproportionate share of their income on food — a category that includes many recent immigrants and households supporting dependents abroad — the compounding effect is real.

The personal savings rate in the United States has fallen to approximately 4 per cent, less than half of what it was during the pandemic stimulus period. Wage growth, at 3.5 per cent, is now running below the rate of consumer price increases. "Households do have less of a cushion now than they did two, three years ago," economist Augustine Faucher of PNC Financial Services told reporters. "That means that this higher inflation is going to pinch more than it would have."

## The Diaspora Dimension

For NRI families, the pain has an additional layer. The Indian rupee has weakened against the dollar during the oil shock, which in theory makes remittances more valuable. But in practice, the higher cost of daily life in America — gas, groceries, insurance, utilities — is eating into the surplus that was available to send home.

Families that were sending $500 or $1,000 a month to parents, siblings, or dependents in India are finding that the same income buys less in America, leaving less to transfer. The cost of a round-trip flight to India, heavily influenced by jet fuel surcharges, has also risen by 15 to 25 per cent on most routes since the war began.

For families with children in college — a common profile in the South Asian diaspora — the squeeze is particularly acute. Tuition is fixed. Rent is fixed. The commute to campus or to work is fixed. Gasoline is the variable that absorbs the shock, and there is a limit to how much it can absorb before something else gives.

## What Comes Next

The trajectory of gas prices depends almost entirely on the outcome of negotiations between the United States and Iran. A 60-day ceasefire framework was reportedly close to being finalised last week, but on Monday, Iran's state-affiliated Tasnim news agency reported that Tehran is halting all communication with Washington until Israel fully withdraws from Lebanon. Oil prices surged more than 7 per cent on the news, with WTI crude approaching $94 a barrel and Brent crude trading above $97.

An Exxon Mobil executive warned last week that global oil inventories are approaching "unheard of" lows and that prices could reach $160 a barrel if the supply squeeze continues.

For families already budgeting at the margins, that scenario does not require imagination. It requires preparation. Carpooling, consolidating errands, reassessing commute patterns, and reviewing household energy costs are not luxuries. They are the immediate arithmetic of a summer that is about to get significantly more expensive.

The war in the Middle East may feel distant. The price at the pump does not.
